Class ThreadRuntime

java.lang.Object
io.github.jabrena.juno.backend.runtime.ThreadRuntime
public final class ThreadRuntime extends Object
The C++ source of the java.lang.Thread runtime in the generated shim: threads, each on a stack of its own, time-sliced by the scheduler (scheduler(boolean, boolean, int, String, String, boolean, boolean, boolean, boolean, boolean, int, int)) every JUNO_TIME_SLICE_MILLIS. Virtual threads and main are preemptive, as described below. StructuredTaskScope subtasks are cooperative: the tick never interrupts one, it gives the CPU up only where the program already pauses (a loop backedge once its slice is over, sleep/yield/Delay, join, a contended monitor), so a statement of a subtask is never interrupted halfway.

On the Thumb-2 boards preemption is asynchronous: a periodic tick (SysTick on the UNO R4, a Zephyr k_timer on the UNO Q) interrupts whatever runs. When the interrupted instruction belongs to the generated Java code (between juno_java_code_start and juno_java_code_end) the tick rewrites the exception frame's return address so that, the moment the interrupt returns, the thread enters juno_preempt_trampoline: it saves every register the interrupted code may be using (the caller-saved core registers, the flags, s0-s15 and FPSCR), switches to the next runnable thread like Thread.yield, and later restores all of it and resumes exactly where the tick struck. A thread is therefore preempted between any two instructions of generated code, inside a loop or not, unless it is a cooperative subtask.

The runtime itself (the arena, the collector, the pending-exception slot, monitors, atomics, the scheduler and every core library the shim calls) is never preempted part-way: a tick that lands outside generated code only marks a switch as due, and the thread takes it at its next loop backedge or when the next tick finds it back in Java code. So none of that state needs locking; the collector scans every live thread's stack, which for a preempted thread includes the registers the trampoline saved, and the pending exception and scoped-value bindings are swapped on each switch.

The UNO WiFi Rev2 (AVR) cannot be interrupted at an arbitrary instruction: a reference or int is loaded and stored a byte at a time, and generated calls pass arguments through one global area. Its threads are preempted at safepoints instead: on every loop backedge and every method entry the running thread hands over the CPU once its time slice has expired, so neither a spinning loop nor a loop-free recursion can starve the others. A cooperative subtask skips the method-entry safepoints.

Only how a stack is created, how control moves between two of them and where the tick comes from differ per board; that lives in the CoreRuntime's port (renesasPort(int, int), zephyrPort(int, int), esp32Port(int, int), avrPort(int, int)): the UNO R4 has no RTOS, so a few lines of assembly swap stack pointers; the UNO Q already runs on Zephyr and the Nano ESP32 on FreeRTOS, whose own threads carry the stacks while a baton semaphore keeps exactly one of them running Java code. The Nano ESP32 is preempted at safepoints, like AVR.

    • avrPort

      public String avrPort(int maxThreads, int stackBytes)
      The UNO WiFi Rev2's port: like the UNO R4's, its own stacks and a context switch, here saving avr-gcc's call-saved registers (r2-r17 and the frame pointer Y) before swapping SP. The return address a fresh stack starts from is two bytes on the ATmega4809 and three on a part with more than 128 KB of flash, which the simulator's ATmega2560 is.

      A task's stack is small and sits next to the scheduler's own state, so a deep recursion must stop before it writes past the stack: every generated function compares its new SP with juno_stack_limit, which keeps JUNO_STACK_GUARD_BYTES free for the C calls of the deepest frame and for reporting the overflow.

    • zephyrPort

      public String zephyrPort(int maxThreads, int stackBytes)
      The UNO Q's port: every Juno thread is a Zephyr thread, but each parks on its own semaphore and only the one holding the baton runs Java code, so the runtime needs no other locking. The preemption tick is a Zephyr k_timer, whose expiry runs in the system clock's interrupt: Zephyr threads run on the process stack, so psp holds the interrupted thread's exception frame.

    • esp32Port

      public String esp32Port(int maxThreads, int stackBytes)
      The Nano ESP32's port: like the UNO Q's, every Juno thread is an RTOS task (here FreeRTOS, which the arduino:esp32 core already runs) parked on its own baton semaphore, so only the baton holder runs Java code. There is no asynchronous tick: the backend emits safepoints, as on AVR.

    • zephyrIoWorker

      public String zephyrIoWorker()
      The UNO Q's I/O worker (CoreRuntime.ioWorker()), emitted after its thread port when the program makes waiting device calls.
